title: A principal localization of a one-dimensional local domain is its fraction field
statement: Let B be a local integral domain of Krull dimension 1 [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], let K=Frac(B) be its fraction field, and let 0\ne f belong to the maximal ideal of B. Let B_f denote the localization away from f [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. Then the localization map B_f\to K is an isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, Lemmas Tags 00CM and 00C8 (localization and the prime correspondence for a localization)

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak m$ be the unique maximal ideal of the local ring $B$. Since $B$ is a domain, $(0)$ is prime. If a prime $\mathfrak q$ is nonzero, then $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak q$; the dimension-one hypothesis, interpreted through the definition of Krull dimension, rules out any further strict prime inclusion above $\mathfrak q$, so $\mathfrak q$ is maximal. Locality then gives $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak m$. Thus the only primes of $B$ are $(0)$ and $\mathfrak m$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemmas Tags 00CM and 00C8; the prime-chain argument specializes the definition of Krull dimension

proof.text: Apply the prime correspondence for localization [lem-weil-pbc-primes-of-localization](2) with $R=B$, $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak m$ and $t=f$: since $B$ is local, every element outside $\mathfrak m$ is a unit, so the localization map $B\to B_{\mathfrak m}$ is an isomorphism and $A=B_{\mathfrak m}$ is $B$ itself, with $A[1/f]=B_f$. Thus the primes of $B_f$ correspond, by contraction, to the primes of $B$ not containing $f$. The maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ is excluded because $f\in\mathfrak m$, while $(0)$ is allowed because $f\ne0$ and $B$ is a domain. Hence $(0)$ is the only prime of $B_f$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00C8 (prime correspondence for a localization), with the powers of $f$

proof.text: The localization $B_f$ is a domain because $B$ is a domain and $f\ne0$, and its only prime is $(0)$. If a nonzero element of $B_f$ were not a unit, it would lie in a maximal ideal, which would be a nonzero prime; therefore every nonzero element is a unit and $B_f$ is a field. The localization map into $K=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ is injective (a power of the nonzero element $f$ cannot annihilate a nonzero numerator). Since $B_f$ is a field containing the image of $B$, every fraction $a/b$ with $0\ne b\in B$ belongs to $B_f$ because the image of $b$ is nonzero and hence invertible. Thus the injective localization map $B_f\to K$ is surjective and is an isomorphism.
